subject: Biochemistry
vignette: A 46-year-old man is evaluated for yellow-orange creases on his palms and tuberous xanthomas on his elbows. Total cholesterol is 480 mg/dL, triglycerides are 620 mg/dL, and lipoprotein electrophoresis shows a broad beta band with increased intermediate-density lipoprotein. His HDL cholesterol is 28 mg/dL, and he had a myocardial infarction at age 44; he has no tendon xanthomas.
question: Which of the following apolipoprotein abnormalities is most likely present in this patient?

options.text: A mutant apolipoprotein B-100 that cannot bind the LDL receptor

explanation_correct: Apolipoprotein E mediates hepatic uptake of remnant particles, including chylomicron remnants, VLDL remnants, and IDL. A defective apolipoprotein E causes type III dysbetalipoproteinemia, in which remnants accumulate and produce a broad beta band on electrophoresis along with palmar xanthomas, tuberoeruptive xanthomas, and premature atherosclerosis.

explanation_incorrect.A: Apolipoprotein A-I deficiency lowers HDL cholesterol but does not cause remnant accumulation or palmar xanthomas.
explanation_incorrect.B: Defective apolipoprotein B-48 impairs chylomicron secretion and is associated with low lipid levels rather than a broad beta band.
explanation_incorrect.C: Apolipoprotein C-II deficiency impairs lipoprotein lipase activity and causes type I hyperchylomicronemia with a creamy supernatant.
explanation_incorrect.E: A mutant apolipoprotein B-100 that cannot bind its receptor causes type IIa familial hypercholesterolemia, dominated by high LDL and tendon xanthomas.

educationalObjective: Type III dysbetalipoproteinemia is caused by defective apolipoprotein E, with remnant accumulation, palmar xanthomas, and premature atherosclerosis.
